strengths: Well-motivated problem with concrete evidence from real ChatGPT traces showing 3x load variation within minutes
Sound technical approach with balanced design choices: layer-granularity preemption, incremental KV cache checkpointing, and SLO-aware scheduling are sensible and well-justified
Clear presentation with detailed algorithms, comprehensive figures (especially Figure 4), and thorough implementation discussion (4165 LoC built on vLLM)

Comprehensive single-GPU evaluation including real-world trace (BurstGPT), document summarization workload, synthetic loads with configurable burstiness, and ablation studies showing individual component contributions
Demonstrates significant practical improvements: 2.35x higher throughput vs. online-only serving while maintaining SLO compliance, and 84x latency reduction vs. naive co-serving
Practical engineering considerations including tensor/pipeline parallelism support, asynchronous I/O overlapping, and adaptive checkpointing policies
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only 1 GPU evaluated (production uses 8+), single model (Llama-2-7B), single offline workload type (document summarization). Results may not generalize to realistic multi-GPU deployments or other LLM scales

Baseline comparison limitations: vLLM++ is a strawman in-house baseline with naive priority scheduling; no empirical comparison with mentioned related systems (DistServe, Splitwise, Llumnix); 84x improvement claim is against naive co-location, not state-of-the-art alternatives

Preemption cost analysis incomplete: safepoint overhead measured (988µs) but actual preemption recovery cost not characterized; no quantification of tail latency impact when preemptions occur during bursts; 3.99ms instrumentation overhead assumes zero preemptions

Adaptive checkpointing policy lacks rigor: 50% memory threshold and gradual rate increase are heuristic-based without formal analysis; no proof that checkpointing rate guarantees memory safety; fallback to discarding KV caches is reactive and may cause SLO violations
Profiling dependency: requires offline profiling before deployment and must be rerun for new models/hardware; profiling overhead and update frequency not discussed; limits practical deployability

Design parameter choices lack justification: why 8-layer batching? Why 50% memory threshold? No sensitivity analysis or ablation studies for these critical hyperparameters; unclear how choices generalize across different architectures

Algorithm specification gaps: relationship between token budget and request count budget in SLOAWARESCHEDULE unclear; priority handling under contention not specified; chunked prefill integration with preemption not explained

Missing evaluations: no multi-GPU analysis, no evaluation on larger models (70B), limited offline workload diversity, no comparison with related systems, no sensitivity analysis for design parameters, no failure case analysis

strengths: Addresses practical and timely problem of GPU underutilization in LLM serving with real-world motivation (BurstGPT traces)
Novel incremental checkpointing mechanism that cleverly exploits the stateless nature of LLM KV caches to enable asynchronous per-iteration checkpoint/restore
Thoughtful system design with coordinated components: layer-wise preemption for responsiveness, background prefetching for efficiency, and SLO-aware scheduling for correctness
Concrete implementation on vLLM (4165 LoC) demonstrates feasibility and enables reproducibility of core mechanisms
Clear presentation with well-designed algorithms and informative figures (especially Figure 4 resume strategies comparison)
Achieves substantial improvements on tested configuration (2.35× throughput vs. vLLM, 84× latency reduction vs. naive colocation)
weaknesses: Critically limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to single model (Llama-2-7B), single GPU type (A100), single GPU instance, and single datacenter node. No evidence of scalability to multi-GPU deployments despite claims of tensor/pipeline parallelism support

Weak and insufficient baselines: vLLM Online-Only is handicapped by design; vLLM++ strawman priority scheduler lacks rigor. Missing comparisons with other co-serving systems (Llumnix), disaggregated approaches (claimed compatible), and simple static partitioning baselines

Limited novelty: preemption and checkpointing are standard OS concepts; continuous batching and chunked prefill are from prior LLM work (Orca, Sarathi-Serve). Main contribution is engineering adaptation rather than novel technical insight

Insufficient ablation studies: checkpointing threshold (50%) lacks justification, preemption granularity (8 layers) unjustified, no sensitivity analysis for SLO parameters, no comparison of alternative design choices

Unclear practical deployment: profile management (storage, lookup, staleness) not addressed; SLO specification guidance missing; interaction with cluster schedulers (Kubernetes) not discussed; cost-benefit analysis vs. larger separate clusters not provided

Technical questions unresolved: formal correctness of layer-wise preemption unclear, potential race conditions between Algorithms 1-2 not analyzed, behavior under extreme load (when preemption insufficient) not specified

Missing critical experiments: no multi-GPU evaluation; no evaluation on model sizes beyond 7B; no profiling overhead quantification; no host memory bandwidth saturation analysis; no real-world deployment case study

strengths: Well-motivated problem with real-world evidence (BurstGPT traces showing 3× load variation); addresses genuine GPU underutilization in LLM services

Thoughtful technical design with clear engineering justifications: layer-granularity preemption balances responsiveness and overhead, incremental checkpointing cleverly exploits autoregressive LLM properties
Strong empirical results on real workloads: 2.35× throughput improvement while maintaining online latency SLOs, with comprehensive ablation study demonstrating contribution of each component
Solid implementation foundation with reproducibility details: built on vLLM, 4165 lines of code, clear description of synchronization mechanisms and CUDA stream management
Clear presentation and logical flow: well-structured progression from motivation through problem demonstration to design solutions with informative figures
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope significantly reduces generalizability: only single A100 GPU tested despite claims about tensor/pipeline parallelism support; only Llama-2-7B evaluated across diverse model sizes and architectures

Somewhat strawman baseline: vLLM++ implemented by authors as priority scheduler; high-throughput baseline violates SLOs dramatically (83.8s TTFT), making comparison somewhat unfair; missing comparisons with other recent co-scheduling approaches

Profiler dependency limits practical deployment: offline profiling required for each hardware configuration; paper lacks analysis of profiler error tolerance, generalization to new setups, or handling of execution variance from GPU features (DVFS, power gating)

Incomplete analysis of system tradeoffs: incremental checkpointing memory overhead and scalability to many concurrent preempted requests not analyzed; synchronization every 8 layers during offline batching could be problematic for different workloads

Missing sensitivity analysis: no evaluation of parameter space (50% memory threshold, 8-layer batching), impact of different input/output lengths, online/offline ratio, or SLO tightness variations; limited characterization of failure modes under extreme memory pressure

strengths: Well-motivated problem with real data: ChatGPT traces demonstrate 3× load variability and >70% idle GPU capacity at average load, providing compelling motivation for GPU harvesting

Rigorous problem diagnosis: Section 3 identifies three specific root causes (coarse-grained scheduling, iteration-level preemption, request-level KV management) with concrete measurements (970ms delay, 3.59× TTFT increase)

Well-designed technical approach: The polynomial performance model is well-justified for transformer operations; layer-wise preemption cleverly exploits natural computation boundaries; incremental KV cache checkpointing elegantly decouples preemption cost from sequence length

Solid systems engineering: 9,169 lines of production code on vLLM; thoughtful handling of tensor parallelism, CUDA graphs, and graceful degradation; overhead analysis shows negligible per-layer cost (21µs safepoint, <500µs KV gathering)

Comprehensive evaluation: Three models (8B-70B), real-world traces plus synthetic workloads, strong baselines (Sarathi-P, DistServe-P), sensitivity analysis, ablation study, and substantial results (2.2× offline throughput, 2.9× TBT reduction, 82% of optimal throughput)
Opens new research direction: First systematic study of online+offline co-serving for LLMs; timely given industry batch API adoption by OpenAI and Anthropic
Clear presentation: Well-structured motivation, effective use of figures to diagnose problems, concise algorithms, time-series visualizations showing real-time SLO adherence
weaknesses: Limited scalability evaluation: All experiments on single DGX with 8 H100s; tensor parallelism only tested with 4 GPUs; no multi-node evaluation or study of how safepoint synchronization overhead scales with higher TP degrees

Performance model validation gaps: Polynomial form appears hand-crafted without justification vs. alternatives; generalization to different hardware (A100, L40S) or batch configurations unclear; profiling requires per-setup calibration (20 minutes) with generalizability concerns

Real-world applicability constraints: Requires simultaneous online and offline workloads (not universal); 24-hour batch SLO specific to certain providers; fairness implications unclear when online SLOs tighten causing offline progress unpredictability; integration required per serving framework

Evaluation limitations: Real-world workload evaluation uses only 10-minute traces (longer-term stability unclear); baselines (Online-Only, Non-Preemptive) somewhat artificial; no comparison with training/fine-tuning harvesting or CPU-based approaches; performance degrades significantly for short inputs (<2K tokens) or long outputs (>512 tokens)

Technical claims slightly overstated: 'Near-zero cost' preemption actually requires 10ms for 2048-token transfer; 'single-digit milliseconds' conflicts with stated 13ms maximum; 'negligible' overhead doesn't account for cumulative 1.1% latency increase

Incomplete technical details: 4-layer instrumentation interval introduces 3ms overhead but latency tail impact not analyzed; host memory constraint handling only validated on systems with 3.3× GPU memory (unrepresentative of commodity setups); 16-token KV granularity optimality not justified

Limited novelty in components: Individual techniques build on existing work (chunked-prefill, safepoints, KV paging); primary novelty is in combination and application to co-serving rather than algorithmic innovation
Reproducibility concerns: Code not released; profiler availability for new hardware unclear; baseline tuning details insufficient; DVFS/GC disabled for latency control impacts realism

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with convincing evidence of GPU underutilization from real-world traces (BurstGPT); Figure 3 clearly demonstrates failures of existing systems
Comprehensive systems engineering that coherently integrates three complementary techniques across scheduling, execution, and state management
Strong empirical results across multiple model sizes (8B, 14B, 70B) and real-world datasets with clear improvements (2.9× latency reduction, 2.2× throughput increase)
Thorough ablation study (Section 6.5) clearly demonstrates individual contributions of each component; solid implementation with 9,169 lines of code
Solid polynomial performance model with reasonable latency predictions (4% error) and proper profiling methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Each technique is incremental—polynomial model is straightforward empirical fitting, layer-wise preemption directly adapts existing runtime designs, token-level KV checkpointing refines existing mechanisms. Primary contribution is engineering integration rather than algorithmic insight.

Severely restricted experimental scope: Evaluation limited to single hardware platform (8 H100 GPUs) with no cross-hardware validation; only 10-minute real-world traces insufficient for diurnal patterns; offline tasks limited to inference (excludes fine-tuning despite motivation); no evaluation of FP8, INT8, or mixed precision

Performance model generalization unclear: Trained only on Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5; unknown behavior on other architectures (LLaVA, Mistral, Phi); MQA/GQA attention patterns not addressed; cross-architecture validation absent; 20-minute profiling burden undocumented for new model+hardware combinations

Preemption overhead not negligible: 13ms per iteration represents 6-26% of typical iteration latencies; 167.2μs for 4 GPUs with TP; actual overhead depends on preemption frequency which is not characterized; contradicts claims of minimal overhead

SLO guarantees overstated: Figure 6(b) shows 86% attainment at s=1.0, directly contradicting abstract claims of 'strict SLO guarantees'; paper should clarify probabilistic vs. deterministic guarantees

Weak baseline comparisons: Sarathi-Preemptive is straightforward extension by similar authors; DistServe-Preemptive performance poor, unclear if due to algorithmic limitations or tuning; missing recent work (FlexLLM); Non-Preemptive not practical for online serving; no comparison to simple partitioning or autoscaling

Unvalidated assumptions in KV cache management: Assumes host memory >> GPU memory with only qualitative discussion of graceful degradation; no worst-case analysis of host memory exhaustion; interconnect bandwidth assumptions (64GB/s PCIe) may not generalize; append-only requirement limits applicability to tree-structured generation and other patterns

Reproducibility concerns: No mention of code release; implementation tightly coupled to vLLM 0.8.4; offline profiling burden makes adaptation costly; H100-specific optimizations may not transfer; hardware-dependent features complicate generalization

Insufficient sensitivity analysis: Performance degrades significantly for short (<2K) or long (>16K) input requests (Figure 9) with no guidance on applicability; no robustness analysis for model architecture changes or adversarial workloads; no analysis of performance model staleness

Narrow offline task scope: Motivation emphasizes 'model testing/evaluation' and fine-tuning but evaluation limited to summarization/QA; no evaluation on actual fine-tuning tasks mentioned in introduction, limiting practical applicability claims

strengths: Clearly motivated problem with strong empirical evidence of GPU underutilization (70%+ idle during moderate loads); root-cause analysis identifies three specific bottlenecks in existing systems

Well-designed technical solutions at multiple granularities: context-aware performance model (polynomial with <4% profiling error), layer-wise preemption enabling single-digit millisecond responsiveness, and incremental token-level KV cache management exploiting append-only property

Comprehensive evaluation combining real-world workloads (BurstGPT traces, three offline datasets), multiple models (8B, 14B, 70B with/without TP), strong baselines (Online-Only, Non-Preemptive, Sarathi-P, DistServe-P), ablation study, and sensitivity analysis

Strong empirical results with significant improvements: 2.37× P99 TTFT reduction, 2.72× P99 TBT reduction, 3.0× offline throughput improvement compared to best baselines, while maintaining near-optimal online latency (within 25% of Online-Only)

Practical implementation on vLLM 0.8.4 with ~9K lines of code; careful attention to deployment concerns (tensor parallelism, CUDA graphs, graceful degradation); detailed profiling process and reproducibility information provided

Clear system design elegantly addressing three distinct problems; safepoint overhead analysis rigorous (21µs single-GPU, 167µs with TP, negligible vs layer execution); KV cache transfer feasibility well-analyzed
weaknesses: Hardware and deployment specificity: evaluation limited to H100 GPUs only; no testing on A100, L40S, or other popular inference GPUs; assumes well-provisioned infrastructure (2TB host memory, 900GB/s NVLink); scalability on systems with limited PCIe bandwidth unclear

Performance model limitations: polynomial with 5 terms is relatively simple; profiling granularity not specified; model generalization to different hardware and edge cases (extreme contexts) not demonstrated; non-polynomial effects at saturation unexplored

Real-world validation gaps: only one trace source (BurstGPT from single campus); no production deployment experience or long-term stability evidence; offline workload diversity limited to three task types; behavior with compute-intensive or very-long-context offline tasks unclear

Incomplete analysis of extreme system behavior: GPU saturation scenarios and SLO violation recovery not explored; host memory exhaustion fallback performance not quantified; concurrent burst handling and offline task starvation risks not analyzed

Baseline comparison concerns: DistServe-P shows consistently poor performance across experiments; unclear if disaggregated architecture was fairly implemented or if poor results reflect implementation limitations rather than architectural issues; deeper analysis needed

Scope limitations: requires offline batch API availability (not universal); assumes shared model between online and offline workloads; applicability to single-task or heterogeneous workload scenarios unclear; specific to scenarios matching OpenAI/Anthropic batch API patterns

Presentation gaps: Algorithm 1 informal and incomplete (TBT management logic not explicit); no dedicated limitations section; design choices lack justification (16-token checkpointing granularity, every-4-layer safepoints); preemption signal latency ('within 13ms') seems coarse for claimed millisecond-scale benefits
